blocks.text: Lipids are a loosely defined group of non-polar molecules that are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents such as ether and alcohol. They are a diverse group and are classified as acylglycerols, waxes, phospholipids, terpenes, steroids and prostaglandins.
Acylglycerols (fats and oils)

Acylglycerols are composed of two subunits, glycerol and fatty acids. Acylglycerols that are liquid at room temperature are oils; those that are solid at room temperature are fats. In animals most acylglycerols are fats; in plants most are oils, for example peanut oil, corn oil and castor oil. Chemically, acylglycerols are the esters of fatty acids and an alcohol, synthesised by dehydration synthesis (OH is released from the alcohol and H from the acid). The most widely found acylglycerols are triacylglycerols (triglycerides), also called neutral lipids, in which three molecules of fatty acid (the same or different) are joined to a single glycerol backbone.

blocks.title: Ester
blocks.text: An ester is the compound produced by the chemical reaction of an alcohol with an acid, in which a water molecule is released.

items: Glycerol is a 3-carbon alcohol, each carbon bearing a hydroxyl group. Its three carbons form the backbone of the acylglycerol molecule, to which three fatty acids are attached.

Fatty acids are responsible for all the characteristics of acylglycerols. They are long hydrocarbon chains, with carbon atoms in even number from 4 to 30, ending in a carboxyl (-COOH) group. They vary in length and may be straight chains (in animals) or branched or ringed (in plants).

blocks.text: Fatty acids are of two types. Saturated fatty acids contain no double bond in their hydrocarbon chain: all internal carbon atoms carry hydrogen side groups, the chains are straight and the melting point is high. Unsaturated fatty acids have double bonds (six at most) between one or more pairs of carbon atoms; the double bonds replace some of the hydrogen atoms, so unsaturated fatty acids contain fewer than the maximum number of hydrogens, form bent chains and have a low melting point. The solubility of fatty acids in organic solvents and their melting points increase with the number of carbon atoms in their chains.

blocks.title: Mono- and poly-unsaturated
blocks.text: A fatty acid with one double bond is mono-unsaturated; with more than one double bond it is poly-unsaturated.

blocks.long_description: A fatty acid is a long hydrocarbon chain with an even number of carbons, 4 to 30, ending in a carboxyl group. A saturated chain has no double bonds, is straight and melts at a high temperature, typical of animal fats; an unsaturated chain has one or more C=C double bonds that bend it and lower its melting point, typical of plant oils. Glycerol, a three-carbon alcohol, reacts with three fatty acids by dehydration synthesis: each OH of glycerol and the H of each acid leave as water and three ester bonds form, giving a triacylglycerol or neutral lipid.

blocks.text: Acylglycerols are efficient energy-storage molecules because of the high number of C-H bonds in them. They are insoluble because of their non-polar structure, so they can be deposited at specific storage locations in the organism. Animal fats contain more energy than plant oils, because they contain saturated fatty acids and so more C-H bonds, whereas plant oils have unsaturated fatty acids with comparatively fewer C-H bonds. When organisms have to store glucose for long periods they usually convert it into fats or oils.
Waxes

Waxes are derived from acylglycerols. They have high melting points, because of their large number of carbon atoms, and so are solid at room temperature. Chemically, waxes have no well-defined structure and composition: they are mixtures of long-chain alkanes (with carbon atoms in odd number, 25 to 35), alcohols other than glycerol, ketones and long-chain fatty acids. Waxes are chemically inert and, like other lipids, strongly hydrophobic, so they act as protective coverings and water barriers for living organisms. They are widespread as protective coatings on fruits and leaves, and some animals such as insects, birds and sheep secrete waxes over their skin.

blocks.title: Uses of waxes
blocks.text: Waxes are used to waterproof paper and cards, in wax polishes for furniture, footwear and vehicles, and to make candles; waxes with coloured pigments make crayons and coloured pencils. Honeybees produce wax and use it to make the six-sided (hexagonal) chambers of their combs, where honey is stored. In humans, wax is secreted by glands of the outer ear canal.
Phospholipids

Phospholipids play important structural roles in making plasma membranes. Chemically they are derivatives of phosphatidic acid, which is composed of one glycerol, two fatty acids and one phosphoric acid (phosphate). Any nitrogenous base, for example choline, ethanolamine or serine, attaches to its phosphoric acid and makes a phospholipid; common examples are phosphatidyl choline (lecithin), phosphatidyl ethanolamine and phosphatidyl serine. Phosphatidyl choline forms the lipid bilayer of plasma membranes. A phospholipid has two parts, head and tail: the head is polar and contains the nitrogenous base and the phosphate group, while the tail is non-polar and contains the two fatty acids.
Terpenes

Terpenes are a very large and diverse group of lipids. All terpenes are made of isoprene units; an isoprene unit is a branched unsaturated hydrocarbon chain with the formula CH2=C(CH3)-CH=CH2. Terpenes form many biologically important pigments, such as chlorophyll in plants and the retinal pigments in eyes. Vitamin A and rubber are also terpenes.
Steroids

Steroids are lipids whose carbon skeleton is bent to form four fused rings. All steroids have the same ring pattern: three six-cornered rings and one five-cornered ring. Cholesterol is a common steroid in animal cell membranes, and animal cells also use it to make other steroids, for example the male and female sex hormones.

blocks.title: Anabolic steroids
blocks.text: Synthesised anabolic steroids resemble the male sex hormone testosterone and cause the general build-up of muscle and bone mass that occurs during puberty in males. In the 1950s some pharmaceutical companies produced anabolic steroids to treat general anaemia, and some athletes began using them to build muscle quickly and enhance performance. Today anabolic steroids are banned: they can cause serious physical and mental problems, for example deep depression and liver damage.
Prostaglandins

Prostaglandins are a group of lipids that are modified fatty acids, with non-polar tails attached to a five-carbon ring. They occur in many tissues of vertebrates, where they act as local chemical messengers. Some stimulate smooth muscles to contract and relax; others constrict or expand the diameter of blood vessels. They are also involved in the inflammatory response to infection.

blocks.title: Aspirin
blocks.text: Aspirin is a prostaglandin inhibitor, which is why it reduces inflammation, pain and fever.

blocks.long_description: A phospholipid is phosphatidic acid (glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate) with a nitrogenous base such as choline attached; its polar head and non-polar tails build the bilayer of membranes. Terpenes are chains of isoprene units, CH2=C(CH3)-CH=CH2, and include chlorophyll, retinal pigments, vitamin A and rubber. Steroids have four fused rings, three six-cornered and one five-cornered; cholesterol sits in animal membranes and is the parent of sex hormones. Prostaglandins are modified fatty acids with non-polar tails on a five-carbon ring, local messengers in vertebrate tissues.

blocks.text: Role of lipids in life

items: Lipids are important sources of energy (ATP); in fact they are the most energy-rich of all nutrients. One gram of lipid provides 9.5 kilocalories, the same amount of protein 5.6 kilocalories and of carbohydrate 4.1 kilocalories.
Lipids are essential components of all cellular and subcellular membranes.
They serve as biological carriers for the absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.
Lipids are a source of fatty acids, which are essential for various metabolisms.
Lipids act as a mechanical cushion and support for vital body organs.
The lipids (fats) beneath the skin insulate the body from extreme temperatures.

Steroids perform a wide range of important biological functions: cholesterol maintains membranes, helps in lipid transport, and is a precursor of vitamin D, bile acids, steroid hormones (androgens, oestrogens), adrenal hormones and corticosteroids.
